explainedBy: A retail investor slumps in defeat after choosing market laggards over true industry leaders.

storyboard.claim: Retail investors suffer massive losses by picking sector laggards instead of market leaders.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A retail investor slumps at his workstation beside the stark choice between leaders and laggards.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the L component of CAN SLIM: Leaders versus laggards.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualizes the personal defeat of the retail trader trapped in underperforming stocks.

explainedBy: A retail investor in 1954 sits complacently at his kitchen table convinced he can outsmart the market.

storyboard.claim: The underdog fallacy is an expensive psychological trap that leads investors to favor cheap laggards.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A retail investor sits at a table with an overconfident smirk, feeling clever about his market strategy.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the 1954 narrative case study demonstrating the psychological error.
storyboard.addedInformation: Captures the investor's initial smug confidence before the trade goes wrong.

explainedBy: The investor sits at the table hesitating because the undisputed industry leader has already broken out.

storyboard.claim: The investor wants exposure to the aluminum boom but is intimidated by the leader's breakout.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor sits looking worried as Kaiser Aluminum surges ahead on the charts.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the 1954 scene as the investor spots the industry leader on paper.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the hesitation retail traders feel when confronted with an extended market leader.

explainedBy: Fearing high prices, the retail investor buys the cheap third-best laggard instead of the proven leader.

storyboard.claim: The retail investor rejects the expensive leader and purchases the third-tier laggard.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor takes a coin to buy the cheaper third-best stock, smirking at his perceived bargain.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the sequence as the investor executes his flawed buying decision.
storyboard.addedInformation: Contrasts the perceived affordability of the laggard against the true market leader.

explainedBy: The trader rationalizes his sympathy play, falsely assuming a cheap laggard must follow the industry leader.

storyboard.claim: Retail traders buy laggards on the flawed premise of a sympathy play that will automatically follow.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor sits holding his coin complacently, expecting the sympathy stock to follow the leader.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the sequence, exposing the flawed internal logic behind holding the laggard.
storyboard.addedInformation: Labels the psychological fallacy of treating lagging stocks as automatic followers.

explainedBy: The investor watches in horror as the true industry leader rockets 379% while his stock does nothing.

storyboard.claim: The true leader skyrockets hundreds of percent while the investor waits in vain for the laggard to move.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor holds his coin in terror as Kaiser Aluminum rockets 379% away from him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the sequence to deliver the disastrous outcome of the trade.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualizes the acute shock of missing a massive triple-digit winner by holding a laggard.

explainedBy: The cheap sympathy play flatlines completely, leaving the trader crushed in defeat.

storyboard.claim: The cheap laggard fails to participate in the boom, leaving the retail investor with dead capital.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor sits sadly holding his dead coin as his clever sympathy play flatlines in the mud.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Concludes the 1954 sequence with the inevitable failure of the laggard.
storyboard.addedInformation: Emphasizes the recurring emotional and financial pain of buying cheap knockoffs.

explainedBy: The market demands buying absolute market champions while ruthlessly ignoring sector laggards.

storyboard.claim: Investors must ruthlessly filter for market champions and discard sector laggards.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A sorter diagram sorting stocks into two clear buckets: Market Champions versus Sector Laggards.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transitions from the narrative failure of 1954 to the categorical rule.
storyboard.addedInformation: Structurally divides the investment universe into acceptable leaders and forbidden laggards.

explainedBy: Institutional investors recognize inferior management and weak margins, actively avoiding sector laggards.

storyboard.claim: Institutions avoid third-tier companies due to hidden structural flaws in management and margins.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An institutional fund manager points dismissively away from flawed laggard companies.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the underlying institutional reason why laggards underperform.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows institutional professionals actively steering capital away from inferior businesses.

explainedBy: William O'Neil provides a strict mathematical metric to enforce objective stock selection discipline.

storyboard.claim: O'Neil introduces an objective mathematical rule to prevent emotional bias toward laggards.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A retail investor holds O'Neil's book at his workstation, turning to mathematical criteria.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pivots from qualitative avoidance to O'Neil's quantitative screening metric.
storyboard.addedInformation: Grounds the transition from emotional trading to strict mathematical rules.

explainedBy: Historical data shows that the average super-winning stock possessed an RS rating of 87 before breaking out.

storyboard.claim: Historical analysis proves that great market winners average an RS rating of 87 prior to breakout.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor points in astonishment at the historical benchmark RS rating of 87 on his screen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the quantitative RS metric and its empirical benchmark.
storyboard.addedInformation: Highlights the surprisingly high performance threshold required for super-winner candidates.

explainedBy: The hosts pause to define precisely how the Relative Strength rating is calculated and measured.

storyboard.claim: The hosts establish a clear definition of the Relative Strength rating before proceeding.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A trader gestures toward an analytical blackboard to break down the formula of the metric.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pauses to unpack the mathematical mechanics behind the 87 rating.
storyboard.addedInformation: Prepares the viewer for the statistical meaning of Relative Strength.

explainedBy: An RS rating of 87 signifies that the stock outpaced 87 percent of the entire market over the past year.

storyboard.claim: An RS of 87 indicates the stock outpaced 87% of all publicly traded companies over the past year.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A horizontal spectrum diagram spanning the entire market with a highlighted marker positioned at the 87th percentile.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Translates the abstract number 87 into a visual distribution curve.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visually demonstrates that an 87 rating places a company in the extreme upper echelon of market performers.

explainedBy: The trader realizes that high RS stocks are already proven winners rather than speculative gambles.

storyboard.claim: CAN SLIM requires buying stocks that are already mathematically proven winners.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The retail investor celebrates at his desk, realizing he must buy proven strength instead of potential.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Emphasizes the core takeaway from the 87 percentile definition.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reinforces the psychological shift from betting on turnarounds to embracing proven winners.

explainedBy: O'Neil mandates restricting purchases exclusively to top-tier stocks with RS ratings of 80 or higher.

storyboard.claim: O'Neil mandates restricting purchases exclusively to top-tier stocks with RS ratings of 80 or higher.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A trader points decisively at the top tier of stock rankings, refusing anything below 80.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Establishes the non-negotiable numerical cutoff rule for stock selection.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualizes the firm filtering discipline required to keep laggards out of the portfolio.

explainedBy: The skeptic host challenges the rule, asking if buying top performers is merely blindly chasing past gains.

storyboard.claim: A skeptic raises the standard objection that buying high RS stocks constitutes chasing past performance.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A trader gestures with a worried expression, challenging the wisdom of buying top performers.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the common retail objection to buying stocks that have already run up.
storyboard.addedInformation: Voices the intuitive fear that buying leaders violates basic investment caution.

explainedBy: The skeptic cites the standard financial disclaimer that past performance does not guarantee future results.

storyboard.claim: Conventional financial wisdom warns that past performance cannot predict future investment results.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor holds up a printed financial disclaimer, pointing to the warning against chasing past returns.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Grounds the objection in standard regulatory disclaimers familiar to all investors.
storyboard.addedInformation: Highlights the tension between conventional disclaimer culture and momentum-based leadership rules.

explainedBy: The host clarifies the crucial difference between chasing parabolic spikes and buying emerging relative strength.

storyboard.claim: Critics confuse dangerous parabolic momentum chasing with disciplined emerging relative strength.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A speaker explains the critical distinction between two completely different types of price movement.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reframes the objection by exposing a false equivalence between two market behaviors.
storyboard.addedInformation: Prepares the audience for the technical difference between chasing spikes and buying bases.

callout.text: STRAIGHT UP IN A VERTICAL LINE

explainedBy: O'Neil explicitly rejects buying extended stocks that have surged straight up in a vertical line.

storyboard.claim: CAN SLIM forbids buying stocks that have moved straight up vertically for weeks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor points to a steep vertical chart line with a cautionary expression, indicating a forbidden entry.
storyboard.onScreenText: STRAIGHT UP IN A VERTICAL LINE
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Eliminates the strawman argument that CAN SLIM recommends buying overextended momentum spikes.
storyboard.addedInformation: Clarifies that vertical parabolic run-ups represent chasing rather than sound strategy.

explainedBy: The proper strategy targets superior relative strength demonstrated during a quiet consolidation phase.

storyboard.claim: True leaders demonstrate superior relative strength quietly while consolidating, not while chasing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor examines a tight consolidation chart base with a magnifier, seeking quiet strength.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Provides the exact technical condition where relative strength should be measured.
storyboard.addedInformation: Focuses the viewer's attention on the base building phase rather than the breakout spike.

explainedBy: During a broad market correction, a true market leader displays resilience by refusing to decline.

storyboard.claim: The defining hallmark of a future market leader is its refusal to drop during general market corrections.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A resilient stock stands firm behind a shield while the broader market indices collapse around it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains how market corrections act as the ultimate litmus test for leadership.
storyboard.addedInformation: Uses the shield icon to convey price resilience against broader macroeconomic selling.

explainedBy: When the index falls 10 percent and laggards drop 20 percent, true leaders drop only 2 to 3 percent or trade sideways.

storyboard.claim: During corrections, market leaders drop far less than the market index and sector laggards.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A three-way sorter diagram contrasting Dow drops of 10% and laggard drops of 20% against the leader's tiny 2% dip.
storyboard.onScreenText: DOW DROPS 10%, LAGGARDS DROP 20%, LEADER DROPS 2%
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Quantifies the exact price resilience difference described in the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Exposes the numerical gap between vulnerable laggards and resilient market leaders.

explainedBy: Institutional funds quietly accumulate the stock during corrections, supporting the price floor and boosting its RS rating.

storyboard.claim: The leader holds its ground because institutional sponsors absorb selling pressure and defend the price.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An institutional fund manager stands firm holding capital reserves, quietly absorbing market selloffs.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reveals the institutional mechanism that creates the leader's price resilience.
storyboard.addedInformation: Connects chart resilience directly to institutional buying power rather than retail luck.

explainedBy: The investor executes a buy as the proven leader breaks out of its sound chart base.

storyboard.claim: Investors must enter the leader precisely when it breaks out of a sound mathematical base.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The retail investor at his workstation celebrates the breakout of the market leader from its chart base.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pinpoints the exact buy point following the resilience test during the correction.
storyboard.addedInformation: Marks the decisive transition from observation to entering the leading stock.

explainedBy: Traders must abandon the romantic impulse to root for underdogs because in the stock market underdogs lose.

storyboard.claim: Emotional sympathy for underdogs is a fatal market flaw; market underdogs overwhelmingly lose.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A retail trader shakes his head in sober realization as the harsh reality of market Darwinism is stated.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts Hollywood emotional instincts with cold financial market realities.
storyboard.addedInformation: Warns against the common psychological bias of betting on beaten-down companies.

explainedBy: Investors should only back the undisputed market champions where powerful institutions place their capital.

storyboard.claim: Investors must align capital exclusively with undisputed market champions backed by major institutions.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The retail investor points to the champion's trophy, aligning his portfolio with the market's heavyweight winner.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Provides the positive counterpart to rejecting the underdog.
storyboard.addedInformation: Uses the trophy to represent the elite status of true CAN SLIM market leaders.

explainedBy: The discussion shifts to CAN SLIM's 'I' component: tracking the powerful institutions behind volume surges.

storyboard.claim: The 'I' in CAN SLIM identifies the giant institutional players responsible for massive trading volume.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An institutional fund manager walks through a corporate office, leaving massive market footprints in his wake.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Connects volume footprints discussed earlier to the specific entities generating them.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shifts focus from the technical price-volume chart to institutional identity and behavior.

explainedBy: Institutions operate with a colossal scale of capital that dwarfs individual retail accounts.

storyboard.claim: Institutional titans operate with immense capital reserves away from the public retail spotlight.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An institutional fund manager stands in dramatic silhouette, illustrating how large money moves in the shadows.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets up the behind-the-scenes look into institutional trading mechanics.
storyboard.addedInformation: Uses silhouette framing to emphasize the covert, low-profile nature of institutional accumulation.

explainedBy: A quiet, serious institutional trading office in Boston serves as the setting for massive capital deployment.

storyboard.claim: Institutional decisions occur in quiet, professional fund headquarters far removed from retail hype.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An institutional manager sits at a spacious desk in a serene, climate-controlled Boston corporate office.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Establishes the physical setting for the institutional order execution walkthrough.
storyboard.addedInformation: Contrasts the serene corporate environment of big money with chaotic retail trading rooms.

explainedBy: A portfolio manager controlling tens of billions of dollars analyzes trading monitors.

storyboard.claim: Individual institutional managers direct portfolios worth tens of billions of dollars.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The portfolio manager sits intently studying financial monitors containing billions in market power.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Focuses in on the enormous capital under the control of a single decision-maker.
storyboard.addedInformation: Conveys the staggering financial leverage wielded by elite institutional managers.

explainedBy: The manager silently executes an initial purchase of 100,000 shares to begin building a position.

storyboard.claim: Institutions initiate large positions by quietly executing six-figure share orders.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The portfolio manager clicks his workstation interface to initiate a 100,000-share buy order.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the first discrete action in the multi-week accumulation process.
storyboard.addedInformation: Highlights how quietly and effortlessly a massive order is placed without fanfare.

explainedBy: A 100,000 share order is merely a drop in the bucket, executed without public press releases or media notice.

storyboard.claim: Massive institutional buying occurs in total silence without media fanfare or public announcements.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The institutional manager smirks quietly at his screen, knowing his massive order is barely a drop in his bucket.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts the large share count with the manager's immense total fund capacity.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reminds investors that real smart-money accumulation never announces itself publicly.

explainedBy: Over several weeks the fund accumulates millions worth of stock through dark pools and block trades.

storyboard.claim: Institutions accumulate massive holdings over weeks using dark pools and institutional block trades.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The institutional manager continues steadily purchasing shares through specialized block trade venues.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reveals the extended multi-week timeframe of institutional accumulation.
storyboard.addedInformation: Explains why accumulation leaves subtle footprints over time rather than a single explosive candle.

explainedBy: Continuous institutional accumulation builds pressure, moving the stock price like tectonic plates shifting.

storyboard.claim: Sustained institutional accumulation inexorably forces the stock price upward like shifting tectonic plates.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The portfolio manager watches the slow, massive price rise driven by weeks of steady accumulation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Culminates the accumulation vignette with its inescapable impact on market price.
storyboard.addedInformation: Provides a powerful geological metaphor for the unyielding momentum of institutional buying.

explainedBy: Retail investors must face the reality that institutional buying, not retail activity, drives all price movement.

storyboard.claim: Retail investors must recognize that stock price movements are driven entirely by institutional capital.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A retail investor sits at his workstation with a thoughtful, worried expression, confronting his lack of market power.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shifts from the institutional office back to the individual retail trader.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the humility check necessary to abandon retail illusions of market influence.

explainedBy: A retail trader cannot move a stock because even a million dollars is a drop in the ocean.

storyboard.claim: Retail orders, no matter how large to an individual, cannot influence the price of a major stock.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor looks dejectedly at a small coin in his hand, acknowledging his inability to move market prices.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Delivers the blunt truth regarding retail capital limitations.
storyboard.addedInformation: Contrasts the retail trader's small holding with the scale required to move liquidity.

explainedBy: Only the heavy artillery of mutual funds, pension funds, and endowments can move a stock price.

storyboard.claim: Substantial price moves require the massive buying power of mutual funds, pension funds, and endowments.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An institutional manager gestures toward the collective financial power of pension funds and bank trusts.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Identifies the actual financial engines capable of creating sustainable trends.
storyboard.addedInformation: Characterizes institutional giants as the necessary heavy artillery behind every winning stock.

explainedBy: The retail investor's sole objective is to identify the wave created by institutions and ride it.

storyboard.claim: The retail trader's optimal edge is identifying institutional momentum waves and riding them.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The retail investor points eagerly toward the emerging wave on his chart, preparing to ride the trend.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Translates the reality of institutional power into an actionable retail trading strategy.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reframes retail trading from trying to control the market to skillfully navigating institutional currents.

explainedBy: A stock requires at least 20 institutional owners for liquidity, with increasing sponsorship from top-tier funds.

storyboard.claim: O'Neil requires a minimum of 20 institutional sponsors to guarantee liquidity and professional backing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A trader presents the baseline threshold rule of 20 institutional holders for any prospective stock.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces specific numerical requirements for institutional sponsorship.
storyboard.addedInformation: Establishes a quantitative floor for institutional liquidity before considering an entry.

explainedBy: Investors must track high-performing smart money rather than mediocre, bloated institutional funds.

storyboard.claim: Investors must discriminate between elite top-performing funds and mediocre average institutions.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An elite portfolio manager in a tailored suit points with confidence, representing smart money performance.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Differentiates between generic institutional ownership and top-tier sponsorship.
storyboard.addedInformation: Warns that simply having institutional owners is insufficient if those funds are chronic underperformers.

explainedBy: Target funds actively winning performance derbies with 30 percent returns.

storyboard.claim: Focus exclusively on funds with superior track records currently dominating performance rankings.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A top-performing fund manager celebrates beside a performance trophy, marking his market-beating returns.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Identifies the elite category of institutional sponsors worth following.
storyboard.addedInformation: Uses the trophy to visualize the competitive derbies among fund managers for market leadership.

explainedBy: Elite managers aggressively seek CAN SLIM characteristics, creating self-reinforcing buying momentum.

storyboard.claim: Top portfolio managers aggressively search for stocks matching CAN SLIM growth criteria.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An institutional manager lines up stock targets, screening candidates against CAN SLIM criteria.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why elite managers gravitate toward the same leading breakout candidates.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows how CAN SLIM criteria mirror the exact metrics used by top-tier Wall Street managers.

explainedBy: Discovering top funds in quarterly regulatory filings validates a trader's stock selection.

storyboard.claim: Verifying top fund ownership in quarterly filings confirms retail trade selection.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The retail investor reviews quarterly SEC filing notes with a satisfied expression, confirming institutional sponsorship.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Connects institutional behavior to verifiable public regulatory filings.
storyboard.addedInformation: Provides the retail trader with an objective verification tool to audit institutional sponsorship.

explainedBy: A retail skeptic fears buying into a trap where institutions dump millions of shares on retail buyers.

storyboard.claim: Retail investors fear becoming exit liquidity when institutions decide to dump their massive holdings.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A worried retail investor slumps beside a smirking institutional fund manager holding millions of shares.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Challenges institutional following by raising the fear of large-scale distribution dumping.
storyboard.addedInformation: Dramatizes the power imbalance between giant institutional sellers and retail buyers.

explainedBy: The fear of becoming institutional exit liquidity makes precise breakout timing essential.

storyboard.claim: Entering a stock too late turns retail investors into vulnerable exit liquidity for selling institutions.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A retail trader contemplates with serious unease the dangerous trap of becoming exit liquidity.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Validates the skeptic's fear and introduces entry timing as the crucial safeguard.
storyboard.addedInformation: Labels the painful market reality where late buyers absorb smart money profit taking.

explainedBy: A stock featured on magazine covers and discussed at dinner parties has already completed its institutional run.

storyboard.claim: Buying a stock after it achieves mainstream celebrity on magazine covers guarantees entering too late.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor examines a popular magazine cover featuring the stock, realizing the easy gains are already over.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Concludes the warning on exit liquidity by showing where retail traders typically get trapped.
storyboard.addedInformation: Identifies mainstream media adoration as a reliable contrary indicator of an exhausted trend.
